Hydrogel

A B S T R A C T

Hydrogels, which are three-dimensional hydrophilic polymer networks, have emerged as versatile materials with transformative potential in addressing critical environmental challenges. This review aims to explore the clas-sification, synthesis, and applications of hydrogels in sustainable environmental remediation. Our study exam-ines advancements in hydrogel-based systems for water purification, pollutant removal, soil remediation, and nutrient delivery, highlighting the integration of bioactive compounds and innovations in smart and nano-composite hydrogels that demonstrate significant potential for enhancing efficacy in environmental applications. Artificial intelligence plays a crucial role in optimizing hydrogel formulations. Despite their pivotal role in sustainable environmental strategies, challenges such as scalability, biodegradability, and effective delivery of bioactive compounds must be addressed. The establishment of standardized protocols and economic assessments is essential for real-world application. This review underscores that hydrogels hold immense promise for advancing global environmental sustainability-provided that existing research gaps and challenges are effec-tively tackled. By paving the way for multifunctional hydrogel development and long-term ecological impact evaluations through these efforts, we can harness the full potential of hydrogels to contribute significantly to global sustainability initiatives.

# Introduction

Hydrogels are hydrophilic polymer networks that are chemically or physically crosslinked, forming soft, elastic, and highly water-retentive structures [\[1\]](#_bookmark15). Their tunable physical and chemical properties, including mechanical strength, toughness, swelling capacity, viscosity, and specific surface area, enable extensive customization [\[2,3\]](#_bookmark16). Hydrogels are further distinguished by their porous architectures, excellent biocompatibility, and sensitivity to environmental stimuli. Since their initial synthesis and application in biomedicine in the 1960s [\[4–6\]](#_bookmark17) hydrogels have been utilized across diverse fields, including op-tics, cell culture, drug delivery, targeted therapy, three-dimensional (3D) printing, bio-embedding, tissue engineering, robotics, and bio-detection [\[7–10\]](#_bookmark18). Hydrogels’ intricate architectures and chemical composition allow for chemical modifications and grafting of functional groups, imparting novel capabilities [\[11\]](#_bookmark19). Interpenetrating or semi-interpenetrating polymer networks are formed by at least two

distinct polymer chains interlacing or partially interlacing, combining individual monomer properties to produce materials with enhanced functionalities [\[12,13\]](#_bookmark20). The most significant advantage of hydrogels lies in their ability to efficiently encapsulate a wide range of entities, including drugs, polymers, nanomaterials, biomacromolecules, and living cells [\[14–16\]](#_bookmark21). This capacity facilitates their compatibility with diverse materials and allows hydrogels to serve as loading matrices, mitigating deficiencies in the incorporated components. Consequently, hydrogels are particularly well-suited for applications in various research domains, with a notable emphasis on environmental pollutant detection. Detecting and monitoring ecological pollution are critical for both preventive measures and public health protection. Traditional methodologies rely on advanced instrumentation and techniques, such as mass spectrometry and chromatography [\[17\]](#_bookmark22), spectrum analysis [\[18\]](#_bookmark23), microbial sensors [\[19\]](#_bookmark24), and immunoassays [\[20\]](#_bookmark25). Despite their precision, these approaches are often hindered by significant drawbacks, including high operational costs, labor-intensive sample preparation, and

stringent testing conditions. In recent years, advancements across various scientific fields have driven the development of novel sensing technologies. Environmental sensing, in particular, has increasingly incorporated innovative materials such as hydrogels, functional nucleic acids, nanoparticles, graphene, and metal-organic frameworks. The integration of these materials has gained substantial traction, with hydrogels emerging as one of the most significant innovations in this domain, owing to their unique properties and versatility.

Hydrogels are pivotal in environmental preservation, particularly in addressing contamination caused by heavy metal ions such as cadmium, copper, and nickel in water and soil [\[21\]](#_bookmark26). These metals are highly toxic and readily permeable, significantly elevating health risks [\[22,23\]](#_bookmark27). Conventional methods for mitigating heavy metal contamination include adsorption membrane separation, chemical precipitation, and ion exchange [\[24–26\]](#_bookmark28). The composition of nitrifying communities is pivotal in mitigating membrane fouling. Studies have reported a marked improvement in nitrification efficiency (100 % vs. 43 %) and a sub-stantial reduction in residual chemical oxygen demand (COD) (9 % vs. 65 %). Enrichment of nitrifiers is corroborated by elevated nitrate levels, increased alkalinity, and stable pH, supporting the integration of membrane technologies with nitrifier-enriched activated sludge (NAS) systems for superior wastewater treatment. NAS demonstrates enhanced nitrification and fouling resistance, particularly in low C/N wastewater, achieving membrane penetration rates 2.5 times higher than those of conventional activated sludge (CAS) [\[27,28\]](#_bookmark29). Moreover, the symbiosis between nitrifiers and microalgae offers a sustainable strategy for ni-trogen removal and biomass recovery in nutrient-deficient conditions. The inherently slow growth of autotrophic bacteria in NAS leads to significantly lower production of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) and soluble microbial products (SMP) compared to CAS [\[29\]](#_bookmark30). Hydrogels have demonstrated exceptional potential among emerging materials, particularly in developing innovative sensor systems. Hydrogel-based materials are increasingly utilized in detection appli-cations, providing platforms for high-precision, selective, and multi-functional sensing [\[30–32\]](#_bookmark31). Functionalized hydrogels combined with sensor elements such as light sensors, pressure-sensitive elements, thermosensitive components, field-effect transistors, enzymes, and microbes-have been successfully employed for detecting a range of analytes across biology, medicine, and environmental management [\[33,](#_bookmark32) [34\]](#_bookmark32). Recent advancements in hydrogel-based systems have yielded sensors with remarkable performance characteristics, including high accuracy and cost-efficiency. For example, hydroxyl group-functionalized hydrogels have been employed for rapid and low-cost in situ detection of environmental toxins, highlighting their potential for practical environmental applications [\[35,36\]](#_bookmark33). Despite these advances, most research on hydroxyl-functionalized sensors remains focused on biomedical and pharmaceutical applications, leaving sig-nificant gaps in their evaluation and implementation for environmental sensing [\[37,38\]](#_bookmark34). Comprehensive studies exploring the feasibility and scalability of hydrogel-based systems for detecting ecological contami-nants are critically needed.

Bioactive compounds, particularly microbial enzymes, play a critical

role in addressing environmental issues. Microbial oxidoreductases, produced by bacteria, fungi, and higher plants, are essential for the detoxification of hazardous organic compounds through oxidative coupling reactions [\[39,40\]](#_bookmark35). These enzymes facilitate redox reactions by breaking chemical bonds and transferring electrons from a reduced organic substrate to an acceptor molecule, enabling energy generation and pollutant transformation into non-toxic molecules. In soil environ-ments, lignin decomposition generates phenolic compounds, with oxi-doreductases contributing to humification and the detoxification of harmful xenobiotics. These enzymes bind to hemic molecules, copoly-merize with other substrates, or polymerize phenolic or anilines com-pounds to mitigate toxicity [\[41\]](#_bookmark36). Additionally, certain microorganisms can reduce radioactive metals, transforming them from soluble, oxidized forms to insoluble, reduced states. This redox transformation involves

bacterial extraction of electrons from organic compounds, using radio-active metals as terminal electron acceptors, or through intermediaries acting as electron donors. The resulting precipitates represent the culmination of microbial redox processes, offering an effective mecha-nism for remediating radioactive contamination [\[42\]](#_bookmark37).

This review seeks to explore the rapidly advancing applications of hydrogels in environmental management, emphasizing their role in addressing critical issues such as waste management, soil remediation, and water treatment, and provides an overview of the fundamental classification and synthesis methods of hydrogels, with a primary focus on their application progress in environmental remediation, current challenges, and potential future developments. Ultimately, the objective is to underscore the pivotal role of hydrogels in sustainable environ-mental management strategies, aiming to mitigate environmental contamination effectively. This review delves into the critical contri-butions to advancing environmental management practices, while also addressing persistent challenges and exploring innovative strategies to drive ecological restoration and foster long-term sustainability.

# Types, properties, and classifications of hydrogels

- 1.  _Structures and properties_

Hydrogels are versatile biomaterials widely utilized in promoting cell growth and tissue regeneration due to their biocompatibility and ability to mimic the extracellular matrix [\[43,44\]](#_bookmark38). Comprising 3D poly-

mer networks, hydrogels absorb and retain substantial amounts of water through hydrophilic functional groups such as -NH₂, -OH, -COOH,

\-CONH, -CONH₂, and -SO₃H [\[45,46\]](#_bookmark39). The swelling behavior, driven by

osmotic pressure within the polymer network, fosters an environment conducive to cell attachment and proliferation [\[47,48\]](#_bookmark40). Hydrogels can be derived from natural or synthetic polymers and tailored through physical or chemical crosslinking to achieve specific properties, including stiffness and degradation rates [\[49–51\]](#_bookmark42). Their ability to maintain a 3D structure during swelling enables them to be molded into various shapes and sizes, meeting diverse application requirements [\[52–55\]](#_bookmark44). Superabsorbent hydrogels, a notable subclass, can absorb water exceeding 100 % of its weight, storing it within the spaces of the crosslinked polymer network [\[55\]](#_bookmark46). Factors such as the hydrophilic-to-hydrophobic ratio, polymer concentration, initiator levels, and reaction conditions (e.g., temperature and time) can be adjusted to control the swelling capacity of hydrogels [\[54\]](#_bookmark45). [Fig. 1](#_bookmark4) out-lines the main types of hydrogels, their properties and applications.

- 1.  _Classifications of hydrogels_

Hydrogels can be classified according to origin, polymer composi-tion, configuration, crosslinking mechanism, physical form, and ionic charge [\[41\]](#_bookmark36). They are generally divided into three main categories: natural hydrogels (e.g., collagen, alginate) [\[45,46\]](#_bookmark39), synthetic hydrogels derived from petroleum-based polymers [\[51,56\]](#_bookmark43), and hybrid hydrogels that combine natural and synthetic components. Natural hydrogels offer excellent biocompatibility and biodegradability, while synthetic vari-ants provide tunable mechanical and chemical properties for specific applications.

Further classification is based on structural and functional attributes, including hydrophobic associations, chain aggregation, crystallinity, hydrogen bonding, swelling behavior, gelation methods (chemical or physical), ionic charge (neutral, anionic, cationic), and biodegrad-ability. Hydrogels may be engineered for rapid or sustained degradation depending on the application. Crosslinking can be either physical (reversible) or chemical (permanent), with dual-network hydrogels developed to improve pH responsiveness and fluid absorption. Addi-tional classification parameters include physical state, pore size, poly-mer architecture, and appearance, enabling tailored use in both biological and industrial contexts [\[57–59\]](#_bookmark48). Hydrogels are especially

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 1.** Main types of hydrogels and their properties [\[60\]](#_bookmark50).

valuable in biomedical applications due to their biocompatibility, de-gradability, and support for cell adhesion. Semisynthetic hydrogels, which combine natural polymers with synthetic modifications, offer a balance of bioactivity and structural tunability. For example, gelatin methacrylate (GelMA) and acrylate-modified hyaluronic acid (AcHyA) enable customized performance. Hybrid systems incorporating compo-nents such as gelatin or albumin with polyethylene glycol (PEG) further enhance versatility and allow precise control over both physical and chemical properties [\[52\]](#_bookmark44).

Additionally, they can be classified as homopolymer [\[61\]](#_bookmark51), copoly-meric [\[62\]](#_bookmark52), or multipolymer interpenetrating hydrogels [\[63,64\]](#_bookmark53). This classification framework aids in selecting hydrogels for specific appli-cations, optimizing their performance based on desired properties as started in Table S1.

# Methodologies in hydrogel preparation

Hydrogels are hydrophilic polymer networks made from natural or synthetic polymers. Natural polymers require functionalization for synthesis [\[65\]](#_bookmark54), while synthetic polymers provide greater mechanical strength but degrade more slowly. Balancing these properties is essential for specific applications [\[4\]](#_bookmark17). Industrial hydrogel production mainly uses methods like solution polymerization, reversed suspension polymeri-zation, and reversed emulsion polymerization [\[66\]](#_bookmark55). Cross-linking typi-cally involves classical organic reactions, including Huisgen cycloaddition, Diels-Alder, Michael addition, and Schiff base reactions,

which are vital for achieving desired properties [\[67\]](#_bookmark56). Hydrogel synthesis requires a cross-linker, initiator, and monomers ([Fig. 2](#_bookmark5)b), with water as a diluent to regulate heat and purification to remove impurities. Key industrial methods for hydrogel production include:

- 1.  _Bulk polymerization_

Bulk polymerization employs vinyl monomers, cross-linking agents, and initiators (such as radiation or UV light) [\[56\]](#_bookmark47). This method is user-friendly and efficient; however, it may encounter challenges such as high viscosity and heat generation [\[68\]](#_bookmark57). The mechanism of bulk polymerization involves the concentrated polymerization of monomers, resulting in the formation of three-dimensional networks initiated by heat, light, or chemical initiators. Specific reaction conditions often necessitate elevated temperatures [\[69\]](#_bookmark58). Thermal initiators, chemical initiators (like benzoyl peroxide), or photo-initiators activated by UV light are commonly employed as catalysts due to the process occurring within a monomer matrix. This characteristic minimizes solvent usage and reduces processing time, making it relatively cost-effective. How-ever, high energy costs associated with heating can increase overall expenses [\[70,71\]](#_bookmark59). While careful control over temperature and initiator concentration is essential for successful outcomes, the equipment setup remains straightforward-rendering this approach comparably user-friendly.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 2.** Hydrogel preparation block diagram (solution polymerization/cross-linking procedure). (a) A schematic model outlines the key processes involved in hydrogel manufacturing at industrial and semi-pilot scales. (b) Hydrogel synthesis involves three key components such as a cross-linker, an initiator, and monomers.

- 1.  _Grafting_

Grafting involves attaching polymer chains to an existing backbone structure to enhance mechanical properties and improve water retention capabilities [\[72\]](#_bookmark60) The temperature and reaction conditions vary depending on the specific monomer used and the chosen methodology; these typically range from room temperature to higher levels. Catalysts such as redox systems or UV light are utilized for initiation; however, their effectiveness can be influenced by the necessity of solvents for dissolving the backbone polymer during reactions [\[73,74\]](#_bookmark61). Generally speaking, grafting is moderately priced due to additional reagents and solvents required-factors that may elevate production costs based on solvent prices and grafting agent selection. While its environmental impact is modest to moderate owing to potential waste generated from solvent use presents concerns regarding sustainability. This versatile technique finds widespread application in fields such as environmental remediation, tissue engineering, and drug delivery systems [\[75\]](#_bookmark62)

- 1.  _Polymerization by irradiation_

Polymerization by irradiation initiates the polymerization process through various forms of radiation, including ultraviolet (UV) light, electron beams, and gamma rays. This technique generates free radicals that facilitate the formation of a three-dimensional network [\[76\]](#_bookmark63). As a result, it produces high-purity hydrogels without the need for chemical initiators, making it particularly suitable for biomedical applications. This method employs high-energy radiation to directly initiate poly-merization processes in either solid or gel states. The specific reaction conditions are typically conducted at room temperature or lower;

notably, no catalysts are required since the radiation itself triggers the polymerization process. Furthermore, this approach is often solvent-free; however, certain configurations may incorporate solvents for specialized applications [\[77\]](#_bookmark64). While this technique necessitates specialized equipment and incurs higher initial costs compared to other methods such as thermal approaches, it can lead to reduced operational expenses over time. In terms of usability, irradiation polymerization is moderately straightforward but requires adherence to specific safety measures due to its reliance on specialized apparatus [\[78\]](#_bookmark65). Moreover, this method is environmentally friendly as it minimizes or eliminates the need for chemical initiators and solvents.

It is important to recognize that parameters such as temperature, catalysts, and solvents vary depending on the hydrogel synthesis method. Cost efficiency also differs across techniques; bulk polymeri-zation is generally more economical for large-scale production, while irradiation polymerization, though requiring higher initial investment, offers environmental benefits by eliminating the need for chemical ini-tiators. Despite its simplicity and cost-effectiveness, bulk polymerization is contrasted by the greener profile of irradiation-based approaches. The data collection process involves hydrogel synthesis using cross-linkers, initiators, and monomers, along with an evaluation of preparation techniques such as bulk polymerization, grafting, and irradiation-based polymerization. It also includes a review of solvent systems, including water, ethanol, and benzyl alcohol, and their influence on hydrogel properties [\[79\]](#_bookmark66). This integrated approach is supported by existing literature on hydrogel fabrication methodologies. To improve repro-ducibility, data consistency, and reliability, the following protocols should be implemented: adopting established polymerization methods such as solution and reversed suspension polymerization to ensure

uniform properties; applying purification steps like rinsing with distilled water to remove residual monomers and impurities [\[80\]](#_bookmark67); controlling reaction conditions including temperature, solvent composition, and radiation dose to maintain consistency; and using schematic diagrams (e.g., [Fig. 2](#_bookmark5)a and [Fig. 2](#_bookmark5)b) to illustrate key synthesis steps. Additionally, referencing prior studies and standardized methods strengthens the validity of the results and ensures alignment with previous research. [Fig. 3](#_bookmark6) shows the preparation methods of hydrogel and the high-swelling hydrogel.

# Bioactive compounds and microbial enzymes for environmental applications

- 1.  _Bioactive compounds_

Bioactive compounds from natural sources, such as algae and mi-croorganisms, are gaining attention for their potential in sustainable environmental applications. These compounds offer eco-friendly

alternatives to synthetic chemicals, contributing to ecological balance and environmental health [\[81\]](#_bookmark68). Flavonoids, a major group of poly-phenols, include subclasses such as flavanols, flavones, isoflavones, flavanones, anthocyanidins, flavanonols, and Flavians (catechins and proanthocyanins). Each subclass originates from specific plants and exhibits unique health benefits, particularly anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Flavonoids, soluble in water and found in plant cell vacuoles, contribute to the pigmentation of fruits and vegetables. Over 6000 types have been identified, all characterized by a core structure comprising two benzene rings connected by a three-carbon chain [\[61\]](#_bookmark51). Carotenoids, including oxygenated forms called xantho-phylls, are pigments responsible for the yellow, orange, and red hues in many fruits, vegetables, and plant roots. Their chemical structure, comprising eight isoprenoid units, enables absorption of light in the 400–550 nm range, influencing their pigmentation and functionality. Carotenoids are also known for their roles in health and environmental applications [\[82\]](#_bookmark69). Terpenoids, with over 30,000 identified compounds, are the most diverse group of secondary metabolites. Derived from the

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 3.** Preparation methods of hydrogel and the high-swelling hydrogel. (a) Different preparation methods of cross-linked hydrogel [\[59\]](#_bookmark49). (b) Block diagram for the preparation of high-swelling hydrogel [\[54\]](#_bookmark45).

five-carbon isoprene unit, they are classified based on the number of C5 units. Volatile terpenoids, influenced by light and temperature, have dynamic emission rates, while less volatile terpenoids are stored in plants. Their wide-ranging applications include roles in environmental management and biotechnological innovations [\[82\]](#_bookmark69). Polyphenols, high-molecular-weight phenolic compounds, are abundant in plants and play crucial roles in environmental adaptation, such as protection from UV radiation and pests. Historically used in leather tanning, brewing, and traditional medicine, they now find applications in food, medicine, biomaterials, and environmental purification. Structurally, polyphenols feature functional groups with multiple phenolic hydroxyl groups, facilitating diverse applications [\[83\]](#_bookmark70). Microalgae, unicellular photo-synthetic organisms, produce bioactive metabolites with significant environmental potential. Genera such as Chlorella and Spirulina are widely utilized as nutraceuticals and in bioremediation, bioassays, and environmental monitoring. High-rate algae pond (HRAP) systems demonstrate efficacy in wastewater treatment, highlighting their role in mitigating environmental pollutants [\[84,85\]](#_bookmark71). Exopolysaccharides (EPSs) are high-molecular-weight polymers secreted by microorganisms to maintain biofilm integrity, comprising proteins, lipids, DNA, hemic substances, and polysaccharides. They are categorized based on cellular localization, structural arrangement, sugar composition, and linkage type. EPSs, including pullulan, dextran, and scleroglucan, exhibit anti-bacterial, antioxidant, immune-modulating, and antitumor activities, making them suitable for diverse biotechnological applications [\[86\]](#_bookmark72).

However, metabolite reduction and CO₂ mitigation underscore the

effectiveness and environmental advantages offered by NAS systems due to the substantial improvement of the performance of nitrifying bacteria [\[87\]](#_bookmark73).

- 1.  _Microbial enzymes used in soil bioremediation and waste treatment_

Enzymes are named according to their specific functions, particularly the types of reactions they catalyze [\[88\]](#_bookmark74). Bioremediation leverages mi-croorganisms to transform or degrade pollutants into less toxic or harmless substances. Various organisms, including bacteria, fungi, algae, and plants, have been documented as effective agents for biore-mediation [\[89,90\]](#_bookmark75) ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark7)). For instance, genetically modified _Arabi-dopsis thaliana_ expressing two bacterial genes demonstrates significant potential in arsenic phytoremediation. These genes enable the plant to reduce arsenate to arsenate, followed by binding and sequestration of arsenate within vacuoles [\[90\]](#_bookmark76).

- -   1.  _Microbial oxidoreductases_

Microbiological oxidoreductases play a crucial role in the detoxifi-cation of hazardous organic compounds through oxidative coupling, facilitated by various bacteria, fungi, and higher plants [\[39,40\]](#_bookmark35). These enzymes function by breaking chemical bonds and facilitating the transfer of electrons from a reduced organic substrate-donor to another chemical component-acceptor, allowing microbes to generate energy

through biochemical reactions. Ultimately, during these oxidation-reduction processes, the pollutants are transformed into harmless molecules.

Microbial processes also can convert radioactive metals from an oxidized soluble form to a reduced insoluble state. This occurs as mi-croorganisms utilize radioactive metals as terminal electron acceptors while metabolizing organic compounds for energy. Some bacteria employ intermediary electron donors for the indirect degradation of radioactive elements. Redox reactions within these bacteria can also generate insoluble precipitates [\[91\]](#_bookmark77). A prominent example of microbial enzymatic activity in environmental remediation is the degradation of chlorinated phenolic compounds, which are prevalent refractory pol-lutants in the effluents of the pulp and paper industry. These compounds result from the partial breakdown of lignin during the pulp-bleaching process. Fungi, particularly those that secrete extracellular oxidore-ductases such as lignin peroxidase, laccase, and manganese peroxidase, are highly effective in degrading these pollutants. Fungal hyphae allow them to penetrate soil contaminants more efficiently than bacteria [\[90\]](#_bookmark76). Additionally, plants release oxidoreductases from their roots, facilitating the breakdown of phenolic compounds in polluted water. Plant families such as Fabaceae, Gramineae, and Solanaceae have been identified as capable of releasing these enzymes to oxidatively degrade specific soil contaminants. Research on the phytoremediation of organic pollutants has focused on three major groups: petroleum hydrocarbons, explosives, and chlorinated solvents [\[91,92\]](#_bookmark77).

- -   -   1.  _Microbial oxygenase._ Oxygenase, a subclass of oxidoreductases, mediates oxidation reactions by transferring oxygen from molecular oxygen (O₂) to reduced substrates. These enzymes utilize cofactors such

as flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), nicotinamide adenine dinucleo-

tide (NADH), or nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) as co-substrates [\[93\]](#_bookmark78). Oxygenase is categorized into monooxygenases and dioxygenases, based on the number of oxygen atoms incorporated during the reaction. They play a vital role in the metabolism of organic molecules by increasing substrate reactivity, enhancing water solubility, or facilitating aromatic ring cleavage. Oxygenase exhibits a broad sub-strate range, targeting diverse compounds such as chlorinated aliphatic. These enzymes have been extensively studied for their roles in biore-mediation, especially bacterial monooxygenases and dioxygenases. Halogenated organic compounds, which are widely used as plasticizers, pesticides, and intermediates in chemical synthesis, constitute a signif-icant category of environmental pollutants. Oxygenase, in conjunction with multifunctional enzymes, mediate the degradation and dehaloge-nation of halogenated ethane, ethylene, and methane [\[94,95\]](#_bookmark79)

- -   -   1.  _Monooxygenases._ Monooxygenases introduce a single oxygen atom into substrates and are divided into subclasses based on their co-factors: P450 monooxygenases and flavin-dependent monooxygenases. The latter requires NADP or NADPH as coenzymes and utilizes flavin as a prosthetic group ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark8)a). P450 monooxygenases, found in both

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 4.** The process of soil bioremediation [\[72\]](#_bookmark60).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 5.** Degradation of aromatic compounds by monooxygenase and monooxygenase. (a): Degradation Monooxygenase [\[97\]](#_bookmark81); (b): Dioxygenase [\[94\]](#_bookmark79).

prokaryotes and eukaryotes, contain heme groups and catalyze oxida-tive reactions for a wide range of substrates, including fatty acids, hor-mones, and alkanes. Their regioselectivity and stereoselectivity make them valuable biocatalysts for synthetic chemistry and bioremediation [\[96,97\]](#_bookmark80). Monooxygenases facilitate the desulfurization, dehalogenation, denitrification, ammonification, hydroxylation, and biodegradation of various aromatic and aliphatic compounds. Methane monooxygenase is a particularly well-studied enzyme in this category, capable of degrad-ing hydrocarbons such as alkanes, haloalkenes, ethers, and aromatic compounds. Oxidative dehalogenation mediated by monooxygenases in oxygen-rich environments generates labile intermediates that undergo further degradation [\[98–100\]](#_bookmark82). Reductive dichlorination occurs when oxygen levels are low, while oxidative dehalogenation events are cata-lyzed by mono-oxygenase in oxygen-rich environments. Due to the creation of labile compounds that subsequently go through a chemical breakdown, substrate oxidation can result in de-halogenation [\[101,](#_bookmark83) [102\]](#_bookmark83).

- -   -   1.  _Dioxygenases._ Dioxygenases are multicomponent enzyme sys-tems that incorporate molecular oxygen into substrates ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark8)b). These enzymes, particularly aromatic hydrocarbon dioxygenases from the Rieske nonheme iron oxygenase family, are critical for degrading aro-matic compounds. Dioxygenases often consist of one or two electron transport proteins preceding their oxygenase components. Structural studies, such as those of naphthalene dioxygenase, reveal the presence of mononuclear iron and Rieske (2Fe–2S) clusters in the alpha subunit [\[102\]](#_bookmark84). Catechol dioxygenases exemplify microbial strategies for breaking down aromatic compounds in the environment, converting aromatic precursors into aliphatic products. These enzymes, which are commonly found in soil, utilize Fe (II) or Mn (II) for estradiol-cleaving reactions and Fe (III) for estradiol-cleaving processes [\[48\]](#_bookmark41). Their broad substrate specificity and ability to selectively oxidize aromatic chemicals make dioxygenases indispensable for environmental remediation.
            2. _Microbial laccases._ Laccases, a family of multicopper oxidases, are produced by various organisms, including plants, fungi, insects, and bacteria. These enzymes, scientifically termed p-diphenol: dioxygen oxidoreductases, catalyze the oxidation of a wide spectrum of phenolic

and aromatic substrates while reducing molecular oxygen (O₂) to water

[\[39,103\]](#_bookmark35) The existence of multiple enzymatic forms of laccases has been well-documented, with each isoenzyme encoded by distinct genes. The expression levels of these genes can be significantly influenced by the nature of the inducers applied [\[104,105\]](#_bookmark86). Microbial laccases, both intracellular and extracellular, exhibit broad substrate specificity, catalyzing the oxidation of ortho- and para-diphenols, aminophenols,

polyphenols, polyamines, lignins, and various inorganic ions [\[105,106\]](#_bookmark87). These enzymes are pivotal in lignin depolymerization, leading to the generation of phenolic derivatives. These derivatives either serve as nutrient sources for microbial metabolism or undergo polymerization into hemic substances mediated by laccase activity [\[107\]](#_bookmark88). Laccases are recognized as a highly versatile class of oxidoreductase enzymes with immense potential for industrial and environmental applications. Their ability to facilitate redox transformations across diverse substrates has made them integral to fields such as textile dye degradation, bioreme-diation, pulp and paper processing, biosensor development, and syn-thetic chemistry. The ubiquity and adaptability of laccases underscore their value in both biotechnological innovation and environmental sustainability.

- -   -   1.  _Microbial peroxidases._ Peroxidases, scientifically referred to as donor hydrogen peroxide oxidoreductases, represent a diverse group of enzymes ubiquitous across animals, plants, and microorganisms. These

enzymes catalyze the oxidation of lignin and other phenolic compounds using hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) as an electron acceptor. Their func-tionality is enhanced by the presence of mediators, which facilitate

oxidative reactions. Peroxidases can exist as heme or non-heme proteins, serving critical roles in a variety of biological processes. In animals, they are involved in immune defense mechanisms and hormone regulation. In plants, they contribute to pathogen resistance, auxin metabolism, lignin and suberin biosynthesis, cell elongation, and the cross-linking of cell wall components [\[108,109\]](#_bookmark89). The versatility of microbial peroxidases makes them invaluable for biotechnological and environmental appli-cations. Their ability to degrade complex organic compounds and phenolic pollutants positions them as key players in bioremediation strategies and industrial processes aimed at mitigating environmental pollution and enhancing sustainability. [Table 1](#_bookmark9) and [Table 2](#_bookmark10) summarize the key bioactive compounds and their applications, and microbial and enzymatic applications, respectively.

Bioactive compounds derived from microorganisms and algae represent sustainable, eco-friendly alternatives to synthetic chemicals, with broad applicability in industrial and environmental contexts. However, challenges related to scalability and economic viability remain substantial. For example, although flavonoids and carotenoids provide notable health and environmental benefits, their large-scale extraction and purification often involve high production costs, limiting their commercial feasibility.

structure while retaining significant amounts of water are referred to as hydrogel-based systems. These hydrogels can be derived from natural polymers such as alginate, chitosan, and gelatin, synthetic polymers like polyacrylamide, or a combination of both (semi-synthetic) [\[75\]](#_bookmark62). Due to their ability to swell in the presence of water without dissolving, hydrogels have numerous applications.

- 1.  _Applications of hydrogels in contaminant removal_

The high porosity and affinity for water inherent in hydrogels enable them to effectively absorb and remove organic pollutants, heavy metals, and dyes through filtration processes [\[75\]](#_bookmark62). The heavy metals are particularly problematic due to their propensity to bioaccumulate within organisms, leading to severe health implications such as dermatological issues, nephrotoxicity, neurological damage, and onco-genesis [\[75\]](#_bookmark62). In addition to heavy metals, industrial effluents often contain persistent organic pollutants, such as nitro compounds [\[112\]](#_bookmark90), and synthetic dyes like methyl red, methylene blue, and rhodamine B, which severely impact ecosystems and water resources [\[113\]](#_bookmark91). Although present in trace amounts, these organic micropollutants (OMPs) exhibit toxicity levels sufficient to impair immune systems and disrupt ecolog-ical balance [\[114\]](#_bookmark92). The presence of pharmaceutical pollutants, primarily derived from pharmaceutical production and bioactive pharmaceutical ingredients, constitutes a newly recognized category of emerging con-taminants. Hydrogel systems carrying bioactive compounds or microbial enzymes can also be optimized for wastewater treatment by acting as sorbents for nutrient removal-such as phosphorus and nitrogen-while promoting biofilm formation [\[115\]](#_bookmark93), or serving as carriers for microbi-al communities. These pollutants persist in the environment due to their resistant molecular structures, entering water bodies via human excreta and improper disposal. Conventional water treatment methods often fail to eliminate these contaminants, posing an ongoing challenge for re-searchers and environmental managers [\[116\]](#_bookmark94).

Hydrogels carrying bioactive compounds or microbial enzymes

exhibit exceptional potential for water purification, particularly for the removal of heavy metals and organic pollutants, owing to their high-water affinity and tunable properties. Methods for eliminating organic waste are broadly categorized into physical, chemical, and biological techniques, including ion exchange, precipitation, adsorption, photo-catalysis, and aerobic/anaerobic degradation [\[75,117,118\]](#_bookmark62). ([Fig. 6](#_bookmark11)). Among these, adsorption and photocatalysis are extensively utilized due to their cost-effectiveness and operational simplicity. Biopolymer-based hydrogel adsorbents, particularly those derived from polysaccharides,

have gained considerable attention for their environmental compati-bility, cost-efficiency, renewability, and biodegradability. These hydrogels outperform conventional adsorbents, such as activated carbon and clay, in reducing, degrading, and adsorbing heavy metals and dyes from contaminated water sources [\[119\]](#_bookmark95). Their unique structure facili-tates high adsorption capacity and specificity, rendering them effective for mitigating pollution in water resources. Hydrogels serve as a sus-tainable and versatile platform for addressing a variety of water con-taminants, offering promising solutions for advancing water treatment technologies and promoting environmental sustainability. Furthermore, due to their hydrophobic properties that allow them to selectively absorb oil while repelling water, hydrogels can play a crucial role in spill cleanup efforts [\[120\]](#_bookmark96). Specialized superabsorbent hydrogels capable of removing oil from water have been developed, making them particularly useful in responding to environmental spills.

- 1.  _Removal of heavy metals, dyes, and organic pollutants from wastewater_

Bio-based hydrogels carrying bioactive compounds or microbial enzymes have garnered significant attention for their pollutant adsorp-tion properties due to their eco-friendly nature and efficiency. Recent advancements have focused on enhancing the adsorption capacity of these hydrogels through the incorporation or modification of functional groups, leading to the development of bio-composite hydrogels or functionally modified hydrogels with superior decontamination

performance. Functional groups and materials commonly introduced or modified include nitrogen (N), oxygen (O), sulfur (S), carbon-based materials (e.g., graphene oxide, GO), and nanoparticles. The inclusion of such functional groups allows for greater flexibility in hydrogel design and enables precise control over structural and functional properties such as tensile strength, chemical and physical stability, and mechanical robustness. Modifying functional groups plays a pivotal role in enhancing hydrogel performance and environmental safety by improving mechanical strength, swelling capacity, and stimuli respon-siveness, thereby increasing their effectiveness in applications such as wound healing and drug delivery [\[122\]](#_bookmark98). Strategic selection of functional groups can also enhance biodegradability, biocompatibility, cost-efficiency, and renewability, making hydrogels safer for both human health and the environment [\[123\]](#_bookmark99).

The water retained within the hydrogel not only supports its me-chanical integrity but also generates nano-transport channels that facilitate the diffusion of small molecules and increase the availability of active adsorption sites, thus enhancing the adsorption of heavy metals through electrostatic interactions or ion exchange mechanisms [\[124\]](#_bookmark100). The water retained within the hydrogel not only supports its mechanical integrity but also generates nano-transport channels that facilitate the diffusion of small molecules and increase the availability of active adsorption sites, thus enhancing the adsorption of heavy metals through electrostatic interactions or ion exchange mechanisms [\[125,126\]](#_bookmark101). The intrinsic polar functional groups (e.g., hydroxyl, carboxyl) in hydrogels further improve their adsorption performance through physical and chemical interactions with pollutants. Additionally, the adhesive prop-erties of hydrogels are influenced by their preferential interactions with hydrophilic surfaces, both in aqueous and aerial environments [\[126\]](#_bookmark102).

- 1.  _Soil remediation_

Hydrogels carrying bioactive compounds or microbial enzymes have also demonstrated significant potential in soil remediation and sus-tainable agricultural practices. Effective soil conditions require balanced carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and phosphorus (P) levels, adequate humidity, and essential micronutrients. Degradable hydrogels are being increas-ingly explored for their ability to optimize soil remediation by enabling the controlled and sustained release of nutrients, reducing nutrient loss through leaching or evaporation, and enhancing nutrient bioavailability [\[127\]](#_bookmark103). Through the process of bioremediation, hydrogels can function as carriers for bioactive compounds or enzymes employed in breaking

water-holding capacity and biodegradability in soil. Experimental re-sults demonstrated that the hydrogel achieved a maximum water con-tent of 22.6 % after 23 days of treatment, with 47.8 wt% of the material degraded by microbial activity [\[132\]](#_bookmark108). Further advancements include the integration of isocyanate and liquid corn stover with biobased poly-urethane to create double-coated fertilizers. Additionally, chicken feather protein was incorporated into the hydrogel matrix, resulting in a

25.6 % increase in nitrogen-utilization efficiency in corn crops compared to traditional urea treatments [\[133\]](#_bookmark109).

Due to their unique properties, hydrogel-based systems are appli-cable in various environmental management activities, such as pollution control, wastewater treatment, soil moisture retention, and water puri-fication. Their versatile characteristics and compatibility with biological materials render them effective tools for addressing a wide range of environmental challenges. Table S2 outlines the recommended hydrogel dosages for different soil types to optimize their agricultural benefits effectively. [Table 3](#_bookmark12) shows the hydrogel-based systems for controlled bioactive delivery.

Hydrogels offer controlled release capabilities, enabling sustained delivery of bioactive compounds and reducing application frequency [\[119,127\]](#_bookmark95). Many hydrogels, particularly those from natural sources, exhibit biocompatibility and environmental safety, minimizing ecolog-ical impact. Their structures can be tailored to specific bioactive agents and environmental conditions, making them highly versatile. However, scalability remains a major barrier to field application due to environ-mental variability and the complexities of large-scale production. High manufacturing costs may also limit widespread use. Additionally, achieving consistent degradation rates across diverse settings is chal-lenging and may affect compound release profiles. The long-term envi-ronmental effects of hydrogel degradation products require further investigation [\[136\]](#_bookmark111). Therefore, optimizing hydrogel formulations should be a key focus of future research.

due to their pollutant-absorbing capabilities and positive effects on soil restoration. They contribute to soil rehabilitation by facilitating controlled nutrient release, enhancing moisture retention, stabilizing soil structure, reducing erosion, and supporting plant growth as well as ecosystem resilience [\[129,130\]](#_bookmark105). However, the introduction of hydrogels may also disrupt ecological balance, particularly by influencing soil water dynamics. Such changes can affect local hydrology through al-terations in water retention and drainage patterns [\[137\]](#_bookmark112). The applica-tion of hydrogels in soil systems can influence microbial dynamics, alter root development, and affect soil chemistry and nutrient cycling. Localized water retention zones formed by hydrogels may selectively promote certain microbial taxa, potentially reducing overall soil biodi-versity [\[138\]](#_bookmark113). Variations in moisture availability may also impact plant health and competitiveness, leading to shifts in plant community composition over time. Additionally, the environmental persistence of some hydrogels raises concerns regarding residue accumulation and potential adverse effects on soil health [\[139\]](#_bookmark114).

Given these implications, long-term studies are necessary to assess cumulative impacts on groundwater recharge, surface water availabil-ity, and ecosystem integrity [\[139–142\]](#_bookmark114). Such evaluations should monitor soil structure, nutrient fluxes, and microbial community changes. Indicators like organic matter content and microbial activity are key metrics for assessing the sustainability of hydrogel use and detecting changes in soil functionality [\[139–141\]](#_bookmark114). Current methodolo-gies integrate field trials, laboratory assays, and predictive modeling. Plant growth studies assess vegetation response, while microbial di-versity is analyzed via DNA sequencing. Nutrient and chemical fluxes are measured to track dynamic changes, and numerical models simulate long-term interactions under varying environmental conditions [\[143,](#_bookmark115) [144\]](#_bookmark115). To minimize ecological risks, the development of biodegradable hydrogels with non-toxic degradation products is essential. Application strategies should aim to reduce environmental disturbance, and thor-ough environmental impact assessments, coupled with continuous post-application monitoring, are critical for early detection and man-agement of potential adverse effects [\[145\]](#_bookmark116).

- -   1.  _Establishing standardized long-term ecological monitoring_

To ensure the responsible and sustainable use of hydrogels in soil systems, it is essential to implement standardized long-term ecological monitoring protocols. Prior to application, a comprehensive baseline assessment should be conducted, encompassing physical, chemical, and biological parameters such as bulk density, porosity, water retention, organic matter content, and microbial community structure via meta-genomics [\[146\]](#_bookmark117). An effective monitoring framework should include multi-year seasonal sampling to capture temporal variability, stan-dardized microbial assessments using high-throughput sequencing (e.g., 16S rRNA and ITS amplicon sequencing), and functional assays for mi-crobial biomass and enzymatic activity [\[147\]](#_bookmark118). Soil health evaluations should integrate USDA protocols such as tests for aggregate stability, infiltration rate, and compaction supplemented with non-destructive imaging techniques to monitor pore structure dynamics. Chemical monitoring must include protocols for detecting hydrogel residues and their degradation products with analytical techniques [\[148\]](#_bookmark119). Experi-mental designs should include untreated controls and replicated treat-ments across varying soil types and climatic conditions to enhance statistical robustness and applicability. Data sharing through open-access platforms and standardized reporting formats is critical to facilitate cross-study comparisons and future meta-analyses. Monitoring should ideally span 3–5 years post-application to evaluate long-term impacts [\[149\]](#_bookmark120). Ultimately, integrating rigorous scientific methods with sound environmental management practices is key to detecting ecological risks, informing adaptive strategies, and promoting the sus-tainable deployment of hydrogels in soil ecosystems [\[150\]](#_bookmark121).

# Advances and innovations in hydrogel-based environmental technologies

The rapid discharge of contaminants into terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, driven by population growth and industrialization, remains one of the most significant challenges to achieving environmentally sustainable development. Hydrogels, composed of various macromole-cules such as peptides, polysaccharides, and synthetic, and natural polymers, are emerging as versatile solutions in environmental reme-diation. These polymer-based systems, particularly “smart” hydrogels with tunable swelling and shrinking properties, present innovative strategies to address pollution while safeguarding public health and the environment [\[151\]](#_bookmark122). [Fig. 7](#_bookmark13) summarizes the smart, nanocomposite, and artificial intelligence hydrogels.

- 1.  _Smart and responsive hydrogels_

“Smart” or environmentally sensitive hydrogels undergo rapid changes in mechanical strength, permeability, and network structure in response to external stimuli [\[152\]](#_bookmark123). These stimuli are categorized into physical (e.g., light, temperature, pressure, electric and magnetic fields, and mechanical stress) and chemical (e.g., pH, ionic variables, and specific chemical agents) triggers, which influence molecular in-teractions between polymer chains and solvents.

- -   1.  _Temperature-responsive hydrogels_

The ability of temperature-sensitive hydrogels to expand and con-tract in response to changes in the surrounding fluid’s temperature in-dicates that these materials’ swelling and deswelling behaviors are mostly dependent on the ambient temperature. Positive and negative temperature-responsive systems are two categories for temperature-sensitive hydrogels [\[152\]](#_bookmark123). Positive temperature hydrogels, defined by an upper critical solution temperature (UCST), these hydrogels contract and expel fluids when the temperature falls below the UCST, while swelling occurs at temperatures above this threshold. At low tempera-tures, hydrogen bonds in their complex structure form, leading to contraction. At higher temperatures, these bonds break, allowing the hydrogel to expand rapidly [\[153\]](#_bookmark124). Negative temperature hydrogels_,_ characterized by a lower critical solution temperature (LCST), these hydrogels swell below the LCST and contract when the temperature exceeds it. Adjusting the solvent composition or introducing ionic co-polymers can modify the LCST, with higher hydrophobic polymer con-tent generally leading to a lower LCST [\[154\]](#_bookmark125).

- -   1.  _pH-responsive hydrogels_

These hydrogels contain ionic pendant groups that donate or absorb protons depending on the pH of the surrounding environment, with their degree of ionization defined by pKa or pKb values. A pH shift induces changes in electrostatic repulsion between ionized groups, causing abrupt volume transitions. In anionic hydrogels, pendant groups such as carboxylic or sulfonic acids deprotonate at pH levels above the pKa, leading to ionization and increased swelling. In cationic hydrogels, pendant groups like amine groups ionize below their pKb, enhancing swelling and promoting interaction with pollutants through electrostatic repulsion [\[152\]](#_bookmark123).

- 1.  _Nanocomposite hydrogels_

Nanocomposite hydrogels integrate nanoparticles or nanomaterials into their matrix to enhance functionality. Nanomaterials’ high surface area-to-volume ratio and reactivity make them effective for pollutant capture and degradation, even in complex and volatile mixtures. Nanomaterial modifications allow for functional group grafting to target specific contaminants, thereby improving remediation efficiency [\[42\]](#_bookmark37). Adjustments in nanoparticle shape, size, porosity, and chemical composition can further enhance performance [\[155\]](#_bookmark126). Hybrid techniques

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 7.** Smart, nanocomposite, and artificial intelligent hydrogels. (a) Intelligent responsive hydrogel. (b) Temperature-responsive hydrogel. (c) pH-responsive hydrogel. (D) Nanocomposite hydrogel. (e) artificial intelligence hydrogel.

combining nanoparticles with other materials often demonstrate supe-rior stability, selectivity, and efficiency compared to standalone systems [\[136,155,156\]](#_bookmark111). Biodegradable hydrogels are particularly promising as they eliminate post-treatment waste, offering a safer and more sustain-able option for environmental cleanup [\[156,157\]](#_bookmark127).

- 1.  _Artificial intelligence (AI) driven innovations in hydrogel design_

AI-driven methodologies are revolutionizing the design of hydrogels, facilitating the rapid development of materials with specific targeted properties. By analyzing extensive datasets pertaining to material characteristics, machine learning (ML) algorithms can predict hydrogel behaviors-such as swelling ratios, mechanical strength, and degradation

rates-based on formulation and environmental factors [\[158\]](#_bookmark128). For instance, multilayer neural network models have been utilized to fore-cast swelling kinetics, offering valuable insights into the physicochem-ical attributes of hydrogels under various experimental conditions [\[72\]](#_bookmark60). These AI models enable the identification of optimal monomers, cross-linkers, and reaction conditions while minimizing experimental trial-and-error processes. Additionally, AI can efficiently screen vast chemical spaces to identify potential monomers and crosslinkers as well as suitable reaction conditions, thereby reducing the necessity for extensive empirical exploration [\[158\]](#_bookmark128). Furthermore, optimization al-gorithms fine-tune variables such as temperature, pH levels, and cross-linker concentrations to enhance hydrogel synthesis. This ensures that desired characteristics-including swelling behavior and gelation

kinetics-are achieved [\[159\]](#_bookmark129). The implementation of these AI-driven approaches provides unparalleled precision in hydrogel design and ac-celerates advancements across environmental, biological, and medical applications. The transformative potential inherent in these technolo-gies highlights the critical importance of integrating computational techniques with material science to develop sustainable solutions. [Table 4](#_bookmark14) summarizes recent advances and innovations in hydrogel-based environmental technologies.

A critical analysis reveals that recent advances and innovations in hydrogel-based environmental technologies have substantially enhanced the efficacy of pollution remediation. The development of smart hydrogels, particularly those with temperature-responsive, pH-responsive, and nanocomposite properties, offers dynamic and adaptive solutions for environmental applications. These materials demonstrate significant potential for real-time pollutant monitoring and selective contaminant capture. However, challenges remain in achieving scal-ability and optimizing formulations. The introduction of biodegradable hydrogel systems further aligns with global sustainability objectives, supporting environmentally responsible strategies in pollution control and resource management.

- -   1.  _From conventional to AI-designed hydrogels_

The transition from conventional to smart and AI-designed hydrogels marks a major advancement toward more sustainable and adaptive soil moisture management solutions. These next-generation hydrogels leverage advanced material selection, functional customization, and environmental responsiveness to improve biodegradability and ecolog-ical compatibility [\[160\]](#_bookmark130). Unlike many conventional hydrogels, partic-ularly those based on synthetic polymers like polyacrylamide, AI-designed hydrogels prioritize environmental safety through the use of stimuli-responsive and bio-based components [\[161\]](#_bookmark131). AI-assisted design enables the identification of low-toxicity monomer combina-tions and tailored degradation pathways, significantly improving envi-ronmental safety profiles. Conventional hydrogels often exhibit slow or incomplete biodegradation, especially under outdoor conditions, whereas smart hydrogels are engineered to degrade fully in response to environmental triggers such as pH shifts, temperature changes, or mi-crobial activity[\[162\]](#_bookmark132). Moreover, traditional hydrogels generally have static water retention properties, limiting their effectiveness under variable soil conditions (e.g., salinity or temperature extremes). In contrast, smart and AI-designed hydrogels exhibit adaptive behavior, modulating structure, water absorption, and release rates in response to environmental stimuli [\[163\]](#_bookmark133). The optimization of predicted perfor-mance through AI modeling across diverse soil profiles and climate zones enables more effective and site-specific applications.

- -   1.  _Challenges and scalability of advanced hydrogel systems_

Despite notable progress, the large-scale implementation of advanced hydrogel technologies such as AI-integrated systems and nanocomposite hydrogels faces significant infrastructural and economic barriers. Nanocomposite hydrogels, valued for their enhanced

mechanical properties, reactivity, and pollutant-binding efficiency, are promising for environmental remediation [\[164\]](#_bookmark134). However, their scal-ability is limited by the high cost of raw materials (e.g., functional monomers, nanoparticles), complex synthesis procedures, and rigorous quality control requirements, all of which substantially increase pro-duction costs [\[165\]](#_bookmark135). Similarly, AI-driven hydrogel systems depend on data-intensive platforms, sensor integration, and advanced modeling, which, while improving application precision and performance moni-toring, remain largely confined to research or pilot-scale settings [\[166\]](#_bookmark136). Broader adoption is hindered by several economic and regulatory challenges, including elevated production costs, lack of economies of scale, limited policy incentives, insufficient access to advanced manufacturing infrastructure, especially in developing regions and the absence of standardized deployment and monitoring protocols [\[167\]](#_bookmark137). Addressing these challenges requires the development of low-cost, bio-based materials, streamlined synthesis techniques, and the integra-tion of AI systems with existing environmental monitoring frameworks. Advancing from innovation to large-scale deployment will also depend on robust public-private collaboration, supportive regulatory mecha-nisms, and increased investment in applied and translational research [\[162\]](#_bookmark132).

# Hydrogels in environmental management: potential, limitations, and challenges

Hydrogels (HGs) offer numerous advantages in environmental management, particularly in addressing air pollution, soil remediation, and wastewater treatment. However, before the widespread application of hydrogel engineering, several critical challenges must be resolved. These challenges encompass rigorous evaluations of reliability, including reusability, mechanical strength, thermal stability, swelling capacity, and pH responsiveness [\[155\]](#_bookmark126). A key concern is the environ-mental impact of hydrogel degradation byproducts.

To minimize this footprint, hydrogel production is best suited for small- to medium-scale manufacturing units. Developing efficient, safe, and environmentally friendly cross-linking methods is essential for creating biocompatible hydrogels with enhanced mechanical properties [\[136\]](#_bookmark111). Developing hydrogels with tunable degradation rates offers a viable strategy for achieving controlled, environmentally benign breakdown. Incorporating stimuli-responsive elements that degrade under specific biological or environmental triggers can further enable targeted degradation and, where feasible, support reuse or recyclability to minimize environmental waste [\[87\]](#_bookmark73). Sustainable hydrogel design should prioritize biodegradable and bioinert components, utilizing both natural and synthetic polymers that yield non-toxic, inert degradation products [\[168\]](#_bookmark138). Adherence to green chemistry principles, such as the use of non-toxic crosslinkers, avoidance of volatile organic solvents, and reduction of energy inputs, can significantly lower the environmental impact of hydrogel synthesis. Additionally, integrating life cycle assessment (LCA) during the design phase is critical for evaluating environmental impacts across production, application, and disposal

Recent advances in scientific methodologies and technical tools have greatly enhanced our understanding of biomaterials and the mecha-nisms underlying their formation, thus fostering innovation in hydrogel design. The historical evolution of biomaterials underscores the pivotal role that science and technology play in advancing their development. The emergence of nanoscience and nanotechnology has further enriched the field of biomaterials by unveiling vast potential for future de-velopments. This interdisciplinary convergence offers novel opportu-nities for researchers to engineer materials with tailored biological functionalities. The preparation and application of biologically func-tional materials now represent a critical dynamic area within life sci-ences and medical research. The ongoing convergence across disciplines highlights the importance of recognizing this trend along with its im-plications for future advancements in biomaterial technology. Gener-ally, although hydrogels possess transformative potential for environmental management, it is essential to address their technical and environmental limitations in order to fully unlock their capabilities and ensure sustainable development.

# Conclusions

Hydrogel research holds substantial importance due to its broad applicability, particularly in environmental protection. Stimuli-responsive hydrogels, capable of adapting to variations in pH, temper-ature, and metabolite levels, offer high versatility and stability. Their unique properties, especially in polymeric composite forms, make them promising materials for pollutant remediation, wastewater treatment, and soil restoration. This review outlines hydrogel classifications and recent developments, highlighting their potential in addressing key environmental challenges. Variations in hydrogel composition pose significant challenges to the consistent delivery of bioactive compounds, thereby hindering the generalization of experimental outcomes. To improve efficacy and minimize variability, it is essential to implement controlled synthesis and rigorously regulate processing parameters. These measures help reduce compositional inconsistencies and ensure reliable performance across diverse environmental conditions. Main-taining precise measurements, stable reaction conditions, and utilizing high-purity raw materials are critical for reproducible results. Further-more, systematic optimization of component ratios and the incorpora-tion of stimuli-responsive crosslinkers can enhance the hydrogel’s adaptability and functional performance. Future research should prior-itize elucidating the effects of hydrogel composition on drug release kinetics, stability, and bioactivity, with particular emphasis on in vivo models, long-term studies, and the interaction between hydrogels and environmental factors. Addressing scalability is imperative to ensure successful translation from laboratory research to practical applications. This entails overcoming challenges in the large-scale production of smart and AI-designed hydrogels, navigating complex regulatory frameworks, especially for novel materials used in medical and envi-ronmental contexts and evaluating their economic feasibility. Compre-hensive testing is required to verify efficacy, safety, and reliability. Additionally, a thorough cost-benefit analysis comparing smart nano-composite hydrogels with conventional remediation approaches is essential. Field trials across diverse ecological settings are also necessary to validate performance under real-world environmental conditions. Evaluating the influence of soil pollutants, nutrient levels, and extreme weather on hydrogel performance is crucial. Optimizing formulations for specific soil types and climatic conditions will improve their effec-tiveness in agricultural and environmental remediation applications. Addressing current research gaps, particularly in the simultaneous de-livery of multiple bioactive compounds and biodegradability is critical. Structural modification, selection of compatible agents, and integration of stimuli-responsive materials can enable hydrogels to achieve efficient multi-compound delivery for environmental remediation. Consideration of scalability, biodegradability, and controlled release mechanisms is

essential for practical application. Further investigation into the in vivo performance of hydrogels in natural environments is essential for developing standardized testing protocols and improving cross-study comparability. Assessing the economic viability of large-scale applica-tions will also facilitate wider implementation, supporting global efforts toward environmental sustainability.
